readout.note: marginal probabilities of the first 3 SURVIVING wires [0, 2, 4] - the ones the fully-connected block acts on - with survivor j as bit j, least significant first. NOT the first m wires: pooling keeps every other wire, so wires 0..m-1 include discarded pooling controls. NOT PennyLane's order either: qml.probs lists the first wire as MOST significant. Reading the bits backwards permutes the classes by [0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7], of which four are fixed points.

provenance: SYNTHETIC QKD-attack telemetry generated by qsh.qml_ids.attacks; class structure per Al-Kuwari et al. (arXiv:2509.14282). 8 classes = 7 attack types + normal traffic. No commercial-OK real attack corpus exists, and the synthetic origin is why no result here is a performance claim about real links.

training.device_name: NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition
training.note: --seed drives the numpy split permutation and torch parameter init. Re-running this command on a CUDA device regenerates theta, scale, bias and every metric bit for bit: five consecutive runs of each Round 47 artifact, and two independent runs of each Round 84 one (the pre-registered experiment and the retrain), max |diff| 0. That is true only since the multiclass readout stopped using index_add_, whose CUDA atomicAdd made the same seeded command land on macro F1 0.809846 or 0.807781 depending on the run. On a CPU it is not guaranteed: CPU and CUDA kernels differ in float rounding, and a long multiclass run amplifies that.

macro_f1_floors.note: Without a floor a macro F1 has no scale. Uniform-random is about 1/K; a constant predictor scores 2/(K(K+1)), earning F1 on one class and zero on the rest.

note: Variational QCNN trained by backpropagation through a dense state vector. The prediction path applies NO QOTP mask: undoing a Pauli frame through Clifford+T is not implemented here (T X T-dagger is not Pauli), so hiding and prediction are kept separate rather than claiming a correction that does not exist. Simulated, not hardware; the classical baseline above is reported so no quantum advantage is implied.

circuit.name: hur-su4
circuit.bonds: every nearest-neighbour bond of the active register: the boundary bond (first, last), then the even bonds, then the odd bonds
circuit.block: SU(4), 15 shared angles per round and 3 CNOTs (Hur, Kim and Park, circuit 9): U3 on each wire, CNOT(a, b), RY(a) and RZ(b), CNOT(b, a), RY(a), CNOT(a, b), U3 on each wire, with U3(t, p, l) = RZ(p) RY(t) RZ(l)
circuit.pooling: RZ(p0) on the kept wire where the discarded wire is 1, then X on the discarded wire, then RX(p1) on the kept wire where it is now 1; 2 shared angles per stage; an odd register's last wire is pooled into the first
circuit.simulability: not a tree: neighbouring pairs are coupled before pooling, so the survivors are entangled. Simulated exactly on 2^n amplitudes (n = 7 or 8), so classically simulable at this size, and classical data in a product angle encoding is the regime Bermejo et al. (PRX Quantum 7, 020304, 2026, Sec. IV.B) find fully classically simulable
circuit.reference: Hur, Kim and Park, Quantum convolutional neural network for classical data classification, Quantum Machine Intelligence 4, 3 (2022), arXiv:2108.00661
